messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Sculptor
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 75

# The Weight of Stone

Hamid is a 75-year-old Iranian-born sculptor who has lived in the same stone-walled studio apartment in the city for nearly three decades. The walls are lined with his work — figures carved from marble and limestone, some finished, some abandoned mid-form. He is a careful man, methodical, someone who has always believed that patience and precision keep a person safe. That belief shattered on a Tuesday morning eighteen months ago when a construction crane collapsed on the street outside his building, sending a steel beam through the front window and pinning him beneath a section of collapsed wall for nearly four hours before emergency crews reached him. His wife, Fatimeh, had died two years before the accident. He had been, he says quietly, just beginning to find his footing again.

He remembers the sound more than anything — a tearing, metallic shriek that he initially mistook for something inside his own chest. Then the light disappeared. He lay in the dark beneath the rubble, unable to move his legs, certain he was dying. He spoke aloud to Fatimeh. He recited prayers he had not said since childhood. When rescuers finally pulled him free, he had a fractured pelvis, three broken ribs, and a laceration along his jaw that required forty stitches. Physically, the doctors told him, he had recovered well for a man his age.

What the doctors did not see is what Hamid carries now. He sleeps in fragments — two hours, sometimes three — before something jolts him awake. The dreams are not always about the accident directly. Sometimes he is simply buried, in darkness, in silence, with no particular story attached. He wakes with his heart hammering and lies rigid in the dark, listening for sounds he cannot name. By morning he is exhausted but cannot return to sleep. He sits at the kitchen table and drinks tea and watches the window, though he no longer sits near it.

He has not worked in his studio at full capacity since the accident. He goes there — he makes himself go — but he stands among his figures and finds his hands uncertain. The studio is on the ground floor, and the street noise filters in constantly. Every truck that passes too quickly, every distant clang of metal, sends a current of cold through him that he cannot reason away. He has knocked over tools reaching for them too fast, startled by sounds that turn out to be nothing. He is ashamed of this. He was a man who worked with hammers and chisels for fifty years without flinching.

He has stopped answering the door unless he is expecting someone. He has stopped attending the small cultural gatherings at the Iranian community center he used to visit monthly. When his daughter calls from Toronto and asks how he is doing, he tells her he is fine, that he is working, because he does not want her to worry and because he does not have language for what is happening to him that would not frighten her. He is not a man who has ever spoken easily about his interior life. Fatimeh understood him without words. Without her, he says, there is no one who knows how to read him.

What troubles him most, he admits after several sessions, is not the fear itself but what it has taken from him. Sculpture, for Hamid, has always been about trust — trust in his hands, trust in the material, trust that the form inside the stone is waiting and will reveal itself if he is patient enough. He no longer feels that trust. He picks up a chisel and feels, beneath the familiar weight of it, the memory of weight that was not chosen — stone pressing down, darkness, the absolute uncertainty of whether the next moment would come. He sets the chisel down. He looks at the unfinished figures around him and feels, he says, like a man standing outside a house he used to live in, unable to remember where he put the key.
